articles.title: The worst of human depravity was exploited by this scumbag — and he belongs in jail
articles.description: If you were physically and/or sexually abused as a child, as I was, then you understand the horror and extreme discomfort of having the person who assaulted you rear their ugly head in your life. It could be a dream, a momentary thought, or even worse, a picture or their physical presence. Their effect on you is life-altering, and not in a good way. That’s why what happened to Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of Ohio, is so haunting, utterly offensive, and, more pointedly, disgusting. When her opponent released an ad featuring her estranged mother, including the picture and physical presence of the woman responsible for Acton’s childhood abuse, it sent a shiver up the spine of all of us who live with the trauma of another person’s actions. The 2026 midterm election cycle was widely predicted to be the moment artificial intelligence broke American political ads and social media content with AI slop. It was going to rain hell on elections, unleashing metaphorical blood-and-guts ads that would create a maelstrom of malevolence. As trackers reported more than $137 million pouring into AI-fueled political ads, we braced for a digital landscape corrupted by deepfakes and atrocious algorithmic deceit. And wow, so far there have been some real doozies, and you guessed it, the vast majority have come from desperate GOP candidates resorting to distortion in bonkers ways. In Texas, for example, Ken Paxton’s allies unleashed bizarre AI-generated imagery of Democratic candidate James Talarico rewriting the Bible in crayons. The Paxton campaign’s attacks on Talarico are a lesson in fiendish futility. In Michigan, groups manufactured deceptive videos of Democratic candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to insinuate extremist ties. The Mike Rogers campaign’s efforts to paint El-Sayed as some kind of terrorist just never end. And in Pennsylvania, someone used deepfake technology to mimic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro making references to a sexual harassment complaint against one of his aides, not Shapiro himself. It begs the question: Is the GOP so hopeless that it relies on AI as its go-to campaign strategy? Personally, since I follow AI obsessively, I think the tricks and schemes we’ve seen thus far in 2026 are merely a warm-up for the overwhelming onslaught that will be deployed in 2028. In other words, we ain’t seen nothing yet. And I can’t imagine the GOP won’t go full throttle next time. But in 2026, as the campaign reaches its final stretch, the most devastatingly cruel political ad in modern history, in my humble opinion, didn’t come from an AI landfill. It came from a warped, demonic human mind. Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy bypassed the digital chew-'em-up-and-spit-'em-out machine and manufactured his own bludgeon, weaponizing family trauma in a $4 million statewide ad campaign targeting Acton in a way that also bypassed human decency. If you haven’t heard by now, the ad features Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who explicitly calls her daughter a “liar” and disputes her account of childhood homelessness. It should surprise no one that on Thursday, the king of filth and AI slop-sharing, Donald Trump, said Ramaswamy should keep the ad up to “let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable candidate.” What the ad deviously and deliberately omits is a mental-health-shattering reality documented in explosive court files. When Acton was just 12 years old — the same age I was when my abuse started — her stepfather was indicted for raping her. The crime led to Acton and her brother being permanently removed from Arthur’s custody. Acton has not spoken to her mother since that trauma occurred nearly 50 years ago. She escaped that hellscape, and the insipid Ramaswamy has brought all that pain and torture back to her. He should be in jail. This was more than a strategist’s political calculation for a standard attack ad. It dragged unspeakable psychological and physical violence back into the light of day for Acton and her brother. I can only imagine what they are feeling right now. The whole sordid idea reveals a profound and chilling truth about the human element in modern campaigning, at least so far: it can outdo AI slop. Yes, AI is smart, it’s devious, and its limits are unknown. But in a dark irony, humans have proven that AI cannot outthink the capacity for cruelty. When experts talk about having humans oversee AI, one person they need to keep far, far away is Ramaswamy. Translation: If AI is to doom us all, it will be because its human operators took a page from Ramaswamy. While tech-driven deepfakes rely on cold, mathematical logic to construct a fake reality, the people behind the Ramaswamy campaign looked at a real, breathing survivor of childhood sexual abuse and chose to exploit her estranged, unwell mother to retraumatize her on a mass-media scale. They took real human suffering, real familial fractures, and real psychological wounds and turned them into a statewide — and now national — sleazy television ad. From a mental health perspective, the sheer malice required to construct this ad operates on a level of devastation that artificial intelligence simply cannot replicate. At least not yet. AI lacks Ramaswamy’s outsized ego and brazenness. It has no concept of shame, no capacity for empathy, and no intent to inflict psychological harm. It merely executes code. And I know I speak for so many survivors when I say that what Ramaswamy did has made us all feel less safe. Ramaswamy exposed an older, darker threat: the boundless depths of human cruelty. In the end, it wasn’t AI algorithms that degraded the political season to its lowest point. It was his malignity.

articles.title: Trump's full-blown frenzy is a sign his midterm plot has failed
articles.description: How do you know that democracy is in trouble? When neither side trusts the outcome of an election. Let’s say the Republicans somehow kept their House majority after all the midterm smoke clears, in defiance of those blue wave predictions. Would you believe they won fair and square? Of course not. And we already know the Republicans will automatically scream, “Rigged!” if the Dems take back one or both (please God) houses of Congress. There’s your death of democracy in a nutshell. This does not, of course, mean that the republic can’t be repaired/restored. But it’s going to take a monumental effort – and no doubt many years – to fully rebuild faith in the system. My chief worry during the Trump era has been about election hacking at the electronic voting machine level, whether by Russia, the Republicans, or whomever. While there’s been no documented evidence of hacking in real elections to date, that doesn’t mean it isn’t technically possible. I have little doubt that it could happen. At the very least, you know the bad guys are doing everything in their power to figure out how to pull it off undetected. As if we needed actual proof, it was provided on Monday when ProPublica published an investigation quoting two former Trump administration officials. They reported that a pair of political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security asked the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to secretly obtain a voting machine, hack it, and report its findings to the White House. The report said that CISA personnel were also instructed not to inform the voting-machine manufacturer about any vulnerabilities they discovered. Huh? The only reasons for the White House to want to do this is either to find out how to do it themselves, or to use the information to provide purported evidence after the fact of how the rigging of machines led to a Republican defeat. Career employees of CISA thankfully resisted the request, and the DHS appointees eventually stopped pursuing it. But the leaked appeal is itself chilling and raises questions about how far this administration already has gone to make this happen. It also leaves me wondering: just how vulnerable are America’s voting machines to actual hacking this election cycle? There are five principal concerns: 1. Direct manipulation of the machines. This can happen only when someone has physical access to the equipment. Older machines and systems with outdated software can be especially susceptible. 2. Compromised election software. Someone with privileged access to election-management systems could potentially introduce malicious software that changes how votes are recorded or counted. 3. Remote hacking. Most voting machines aren’t connected to the internet while voters use them. But some systems have network connections, creating potential avenues for attack. 4. Insider interference. Election employees, contractors or others with authorized access could theoretically manipulate equipment, software or procedures. 5, Manipulation of reported results. Election-night reporting websites can be attacked or altered without changing the underlying official vote totals. It could, however, create confusion. Given this handful of possibilities, it’s theoretically doable to change the results, but considerably more difficult than simply breaking into a computer. To alter the outcome of a congressional race, an attacker would need to compromise enough votes in a particular district to overcome the actual margin of victory while avoiding detection through audits, recounts and other safeguards. Probably the most important protection is the existence of a voter-verifiable paper ballot, which is the case for 99 percent of votes, both in-person and/or electronic, in the upcoming election. If electronic totals are manipulated, election officials can independently count the physical ballots to establish the correct result. Given the above, while the hacking threat is certainly real, a successful large-scale alteration of vote totals remains pretty unlikely given what we know about the current limits of technology. That’s certainly the case when assessing the risk posed by a foreign hacker. There may be a sizably greater chance that someone with control over government resources could interfere with voting machines/ballot tabulation in Democratic-leaning districts. Particularly given our knowledge of this corrupt administration, the chances of an inside job are more concerning. Obviously, any attempt by the feds to seize the voting equipment must be fought off vigorously. We already know that the Justice Department would establish a pretext of needing to protect the vote from evidence of fraud when, in fact, it’s that very department that would be instituting the scamming. The wild card here could be the crooked Supreme Court if it came to that. What should reduce our paranoia surrounding the likelihood of machine-based rigging is the fact that the president has no general constitutional authority to snatch voting machines, and post-election audits can, as far as we’re aware, detect manipulation. The Dems are also prepared to challenge any unlawful interference via state attorneys general, election administrators and the federal courts (assuming their rulings are still heeded). There are also innumerable pairs of eyes on the process, both directly and indirectly, in the form of journalists, election observers and independent organizations. The bottom line is that modifying machine totals in any targeted district would require overcoming local security measures, and those properly preserved paper ballots would theoretically expose any discrepancies. Additionally – and this is not a minor addendum – there’s widespread understanding of what these guys are looking to do. There is hardly a registered voter in the United States who isn’t aware that the Republicans, led by their amoral leader, will stop at nothing to win. That includes lying, cheating, stealing, and absolutely hacking into electronic measuring devices to reverse a certain loss if need be. What’s galling is this predilection to pretend that the other side has any interest whatsoever in protecting the “integrity” of the election. Who do these people think they’re kidding? On the other hand, it’s somehow reassuring that they’re pulling out so many stops to halt the impending carnage. It should tell us they haven’t yet mastered the art of electronic interference, or they wouldn’t bother. (Ray Richmond is a longtime journalist/author and an adjunct professor at Chapman University in Orange, CA.)

articles.title: Fine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to Japan | Emily Bratt
articles.description: Working in Japanese schools, I saw how teaching young people civic pride creates adults with consideration for others There are two types of people who listen to music in public: those who wear headphones and those who … are a word I probably can’t use here. “Loudcasting” – playing audio, watching videos or talking on speakerphone in public spaces – is a form of antisocial behaviour that drives eight in 10 of people in the UK crazy, and I’m glad Andy Burnham is one of those eight. But while I welcome his policy to fine “headphone dodgers”, I’m not convinced it will solve the problem. This behaviour isn’t only a nuisance, but a grave indicator of a deeper societal issue: the erosion of empathy. You can’t legislate civic pride into an individualistic culture where feelings of social disconnection are widespread. Continue reading...
